idiom_name: embedded noCopy sentinel (Lock/Unlock on the pointer receiver) + pointer-oriented API
implementation_notes: The Go compiler copies struct values freely, so the realization is a sentinel instead of a language feature: declare an empty struct whose pointer has `Lock()`/`Unlock()` methods and store it in every type that must not be copied, which makes `go vet`'s copylocks checker report assignments, argument passing, returns, range copies and composite literals of those types ('assignment copies lock value ... contains noCopy') - the same mechanism the sync package uses for Mutex, Once and Map. The guarantee is static analysis, not a compile error, so run `go vet` (or `go test -vet=copylocks`) in CI, let constructors return `*T` and give methods pointer receivers so the value form is never the convenient one, and remember the check is structural: any embedded struct whose pointer implements sync.Locker triggers it, whatever it is named. The classic base-class form has no Go analogue beyond this embedded sentinel.
pitfalls: The compiler still allows the copy: without `go vet -copylocks` running (it is not part of compilation, and plain `go test` does not run it by default) the guard is silent, so the check belongs in CI.

Embedding the sentinel promotes its no-op Lock/Unlock onto the outer type and can make a value look like a mutex; prefer a blank or unexported named field and embed only when the pointer must satisfy sync.Locker.

Any struct that contains a value whose pointer implements sync.Locker is reported too, so warnings may name an inner sync.Mutex rather than your sentinel - read the 'contains ...' path before assuming a false positive.
Pointers are copyable, so a pointer-oriented API relocates the problem to aliasing; decide and document who owns the `*T` and keep the pointer in one place.
